This is stretching my knowledge a bit, but.

For an electric motor, the torque developed is a direct linear relationship between voltage, RPM, and torque. In the simplest case of a brushed DC motor, at a given voltage V, the engine can either get up to a rotational speed S, or can put out a torque T, where S+T = V (with some constants in there and such, this is qualitative not quantitative.) So, if the motor is heavily loaded, it puts out a lot of torque at a low speed, and if it is lightly loaded the speed goes way up, the torque goes down, and the power consumed goes down.

This works because you can directly control and adjust the voltage in a very controlled fashion. As an aside, in general an electric motor will last longer than an ICE.

A combustion engine generally works off of a much higher number of fixed variables. Fuel type, number of cylinders, compression ratios, fuel to air ratios, cylinder geometries, turbochargers, etc. Also, heat (thermodynamically gasoline = heat for this discussion) is a high entropy energy source, vs electricity which is one of the lowest entropy forms of energy. These don't interact in simple linear ways, so you invariably get a situation where the engine has a specific set of conditions that are the best tradeoffs between all of the variables.
